strengths: Significance: Text-controlled completion under ambiguous observations is a useful problem. Separating visible-evidence preservation from semantic control of unseen regions provides a practical interface for generating alternative plausible 3D assets.

Originality: The combination of multiple visual priors, attention-logit smoothing, and visibility-aware velocity blending is a useful methodological contribution. Its training-free application to both SAM3D and TRELLIS increases its practical relevance.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements across both backbones. On SAM3D, Point-FID improves from 100.38 to 81.11 and CLIP-text from 24.08 to 27.26. Qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful semantic branching, and the reported user preferences strongly favor RelaxFlow.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and qualitative comparisons are understandable. Appendix E provides concrete visibility-mask parameters, and Appendix G appropriately acknowledges failures when observation and prior conflict. I identify no material ethical concern in the proposed application itself.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical equivalence is unsupported. The abstract and contributions claim that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field. Appendix A.4 establishes only a Lipschitz bound on the velocity change caused by perturbing logits. This does not establish convolution of the velocity field, attenuation of its high-frequency components, or equivalence between smoothing token indices and smoothing over latent states. Consequently, the field-level analysis does not justify the implemented mechanism as claimed.

Soundness—the error-reduction and stability proofs contain substantive gaps. Proposition A.4 neglects the signal bias introduced by Gaussian filtering: band limitation does not make a Gaussian preserve all low-frequency components exactly, and high-frequency dominance of the error alone does not guarantee that error reduction outweighs signal distortion. It also transfers a spatial L2 argument to a trajectory-integrated error without justification. Lemma A.7 incorrectly takes the time-varying alpha_t outside integrals over earlier times; Theorem A.8 likewise cannot bound the observation contribution using 1-alpha_max. Finally, a smaller Wasserstein upper bound does not establish a smaller actual distance, contrary to the accompanying claims.

Observation preservation is neither guaranteed by the method nor adequately measured. Following an observation-conditioned learned velocity does not impose a hard pixel constraint, and the sparse-structure stage can change visible geometry. Appendix E estimates self-visibility from generated voxels but does not describe incorporating the external occluder or observed-object mask. Moreover, minimum LPIPS selects the best of ten rendered views rather than testing masked fidelity at the observed camera; CLIP-image measures semantic agreement with a reference set. Neither establishes the repeatedly claimed strict preservation of visible evidence.

An important experimental inconsistency remains unresolved. Section 5.2 says ExtremeOcc-3D uses RelaxFlow only at the geometry stage, while Section 4.3 introduces visibility-aware blending specifically for SLAT. Nevertheless, Figure 5 attributes a substantial ExtremeOcc-3D improvement to this mask, from Point-FID 92.3 to 81.1. The manuscript needs to specify which stages and masks actually produced these results.

Evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the proposed contributions. The main ExtremeOcc-3D comparisons give RelaxFlow category-derived priors while several baselines lack comparable semantic control. Component ablations provide some evidence, but a complete comparison against simple prior-conditioned velocity blending under identical inputs and compute is missing. AmbiSem-3D contains only 21 manually curated cases, and neither stochastic variability nor confidence intervals are reported. Dataset-level FID and Point-FID improvements also do not establish instance-level geometric consistency.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The filtering criteria reducing approximately 2,000 ExtremeOcc candidates to 264 cases, exact benchmark instances and branching prompts, solver step counts, affected attention layers, token ordering and blur-boundary handling, and precise Point-E feature extraction are insufficiently specified. The 32-person study omits important presentation, randomization, aggregation, and consent details. These omissions limit independent verification of both the automatic and human evaluations.

Significance and presentation are weakened by overstatement. Prior work already supplies attention smoothing, composed guidance, and text-guided amodal completion, making this primarily a promising integration whose stronger conceptual claims require validation. The asserted negligible overhead is unsupported by timing or memory measurements; parallel branch evaluation and longer prior-token sequences still consume resources. Overall, the empirical promise does not compensate for unsupported central guarantees and unresolved evaluation inconsistencies.

strengths: Significance: Text-controlled completion under ambiguous observations is a useful problem. ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D distinguish category recovery under severe occlusion from generating multiple interpretations of the same observation.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements on both backbones. With SAM3D, Point-FID improves from 100.38 to 81.11 and CLIP-text similarity from 24.08 to 27.26, while LPIPS also improves. Qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful prompt-dependent completions, and the 32-participant study reports substantial preference for RelaxFlow.

Originality: Combining multiple visual priors, attention smoothing, and visibility-dependent velocity fusion offers a potentially useful training-free adaptation of existing generators. Its practical integration is more compelling than its claimed theoretical novelty.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and qualitative comparisons make the intended behavior understandable. Appendices provide prior construction, metric definitions, and visibility hyperparameters. Appendix G appropriately acknowledges incompatible conditions and illustrates failures; this honest discussion is a strength.
weaknesses: Soundness—central equivalence is not proved: The abstract and contributions claim that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field. Appendix A.4 establishes only a Lipschitz bound on the change in velocity when logits change. This neither establishes convolution of the velocity field nor suppression of its high-frequency components. Smoothing flattened query/key indices, followed by softmax and subsequent nonlinear layers, does not automatically implement the state-space convolution analyzed in Appendix A.2.

Soundness—error-reduction and stability arguments contain substantive gaps: Proposition A.4 neglects the signal-bias term v_sem − Gσ*v_sem; Gaussian filtering does not exactly preserve a band-limited signal. It also moves from a spatial L2 inequality via Parseval to error along a trajectory without justification. Lemma A.7 pulls the time-varying α_t outside trajectory integrals, contrary to the proposed schedule. Finally, a smaller Wasserstein upper bound does not establish that the actual generated distribution is closer to ground truth, as claimed in Section 3.2.2. These problems undermine a central advertised contribution.

Soundness—strict observation preservation is unsupported: Retaining the observation-conditioned velocity at visible voxels does not impose equality between rendered pixels and the observation, particularly when geometry and the shared latent state have already changed. Appendix D evaluates minimum LPIPS over ten predicted views rather than correspondence at the observed camera restricted to visible pixels. CLIP similarity is also too coarse to substantiate strict preservation. A camera-aligned, visibility-masked evaluation is needed.

Experimental consistency: Section 5.2 says ExtremeOcc-3D uses RelaxFlow only at the geometry stage, whereas Section 4.3 introduces the visibility mask in SLAT. Nevertheless, Figure 5 attributes a large ExtremeOcc-3D improvement to this mask. The manuscript must explain where the mask is actually applied before this ablation can be interpreted or reproduced.

Evaluation and significance: The reported gains are encouraging but do not cleanly isolate the proposed mechanism from access to additional semantic information. Table 1 lacks a clearly specified, equally conditioned simple velocity-blending baseline, and the component ablations are incomplete. AmbiSem-3D contains only 21 manually designed cases, while the filtering from approximately 2,000 ExtremeOcc candidates to 264 cases is insufficiently explained. No uncertainty across generation seeds or prior samples is reported. These limitations restrict the strength and generality of the conclusions.

Reproducibility and efficiency: Important details are missing, including solver step counts, baseline editing settings, exact benchmark selections, and attention sequence ordering and boundary handling across multiple priors. The claim of negligible overhead is unsupported by latency or memory measurements; parallel branch evaluation does not eliminate the cost of additional network computation, longer conditioning sequences, or prior generation.

Human-study reporting and ethics: The manuscript gives participant and case counts but does not adequately describe randomization, presentation protocol, aggregation, uncertainty, or consent procedures. This limits interpretation of the preference result and assessment of participant protections, although there is no affirmative evidence of unethical conduct. Overall, the practical merits do not outweigh the unsupported central guarantees and unresolved evaluation issues.

strengths: Significance: Text-controlled completion under ambiguous visual evidence is a useful problem. Separating observation preservation from semantic guidance addresses a practical limitation of image-to-3D systems, and the two proposed benchmarks distinguish extreme occlusion from multiple plausible interpretations.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements across both backbones. With SAM3D, Point-FID improves from 100.38 to 81.11 and CLIP-text from 24.08 to 27.26, alongside improved LPIPS. The qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful changes to unseen structure, and the 32-participant study reports a substantial preference for RelaxFlow.

Originality and practicality: The combination of multiple visual priors, attention smoothing, and visibility-aware velocity blending provides a useful training-free adaptation of existing generators. Ablations support the practical contribution of smoothing, and generated priors perform comparably to retrieved priors.

Presentation and limitations: The task motivation and pipeline are generally understandable, with informative visual comparisons. Appendices provide metric definitions, prior-construction instructions, and visibility-mask parameters. Appendix G appropriately acknowledges failures under incompatible conditions; this honest discussion is a strength. No material research-ethics violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical equivalence is not established. The abstract and contribution list claim that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative velocity field. Appendix A.4 only bounds the change in velocity by the change in logits under a Lipschitz assumption. This does not establish convolution of the velocity field or preservation of its low-frequency components through softmax and subsequent nonlinear layers. Moreover, smoothing along flattened token indices is distinct from smoothing over latent-state coordinates, which is the operation analyzed in Appendix A.2.

Soundness—the error-reduction proof has substantive gaps. Proposition A.4 omits the signal-bias term: the actual error is (I−Gσ)vsem + Gσϵ, rather than simply Gσϵ. Gaussian filtering attenuates nonzero low frequencies even for a band-limited signal, and the qualitative spectral assumptions do not bound this bias relative to error reduction. The proof also moves from a spatial L2 inequality via Parseval to an error measured along a trajectory without justification. These gaps undermine the strict improvement asserted in Eq. 4.

Soundness—the distributional guarantee is overstated. Appendix A.3 takes the time-dependent mixing coefficient αt outside integrals over earlier times, although the implemented schedule varies and has a cutoff. The Wasserstein argument also requires an expectation over initial states that is absent from the defined trajectory errors. Independently, a smaller upper bound does not prove that the actual generated distribution is closer to the target. These are material issues because improved theoretical guarantees are a central claimed contribution.

Observation preservation is neither guaranteed nor directly demonstrated. Leaving the observation-conditioned network unchanged does not enforce a hard pixel constraint: it is evaluated at states modified by semantic guidance, and the geometry stage blends both velocities. The visibility mask is soft and omitted for TRELLIS. Appendix D evaluates minimum LPIPS over ten views, rather than masked reconstruction at the known observation camera; CLIP-image additionally incorporates ground-truth multiview renders. These metrics cannot substantiate repeated claims of strict preservation of visible evidence.

Evaluation scope and uncertainty remain limited. AmbiSem-3D contains only 21 manually designed cases, while the selection of 264 ExtremeOcc-3D cases from approximately 2,000 candidates is insufficiently specified. No repeated-seed results or confidence intervals are reported. The user study lacks details on randomization, presentation, instructions, and aggregation across semantic branches. These omissions limit confidence in generalization and the smaller automatic-metric gains.

Reproducibility and experimental consistency need improvement. Section 5.2 says ExtremeOcc-3D applies RelaxFlow only at the geometry stage, while the visibility mask is defined for SLAT; nevertheless, Figure 5 reports a substantial visibility-mask ablation on ExtremeOcc-3D. This discrepancy needs resolution. Solver-step counts, exact modified attention layers, baseline adaptation settings, and benchmark identifiers are also not sufficiently documented. The claim of negligible overhead has no runtime or memory measurements; parallel branch evaluation alone does not establish negligible cost.

Overall assessment: The practical idea and reported results are promising, but originality rests primarily on the task-specific combination of existing mechanisms, while the claimed new theoretical understanding is unsupported as written. Correcting the theory, narrowing preservation claims, and strengthening evaluation and reproducibility are necessary before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Text-controlled completion of ambiguous 3D objects is a useful problem. Separating visible-evidence preservation from semantic completion offers a practical way to control pretrained generators without retraining.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports improvements on both backbones. With SAM3D, Point-FID improves from 100.38 to 81.11, FID from 50.73 to 39.44, and CLIP text alignment from 24.08 to 27.26. Appendix E includes several additional baseline families, strengthening the empirical comparison.

Originality: The combination of multiple visual priors, attention smoothing, and spatially gated velocity blending is a useful application-specific contribution. The semantic-branching benchmark also explicitly tests whether different prompts produce different plausible completions of the same observation.

Presentation and limitations: The main pipeline is understandable, and the qualitative examples illustrate the intended behavior. The manuscript reports runtime overhead and honestly discusses incompatible-condition failures. The impact statement acknowledges synthetic-content misuse and inherited biases; no material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central equivalence claim is unsupported. The abstract and introduction claim that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field. Appendix A.4 establishes only a Lipschitz bound on the magnitude of the induced velocity change. This does not establish convolution of the velocity field, attenuation of its high-frequency components, or preservation of semantic structure. Smoothing flattened query/key indices is also different from smoothing over the latent-state variable used in the spectral analysis, particularly through nonlinear softmax and downstream network layers.

Soundness—the error-reduction proof has substantive gaps. Proposition A.4 replaces the actual residual, (I−Gσ)vsem + Gσϵ, by Gσϵ, ignoring semantic-signal attenuation. Gaussian filtering does not exactly preserve a nonconstant band-limited signal, and the qualitative spectral assumptions do not quantitatively bound this bias. Furthermore, reducing a global spatial L2 norm via Parseval does not imply reducing the trajectory-restricted error in Eq. (3). Thus the strict improvement asserted in Eq. (4) is not established.

Soundness—the distributional guarantee also needs correction. Lemma A.7 pulls the time-varying αt outside integrals over earlier times. Theorem A.8 then uses 1−αmax to weight observation error, which cannot generally upper-bound its accumulated contribution. The transition to Wasserstein distance also requires expectation over initializations in the error quantities. Even a valid tighter upper bound would not prove that the actual generated distribution is closer to ground truth, as claimed in Section 3.2.2.

Observation preservation is neither guaranteed nor directly demonstrated. An unchanged observation-conditioned network evaluated at a prior-modified state is not a hard pixel constraint, and the visibility mask only gates latent velocities. Appendix D evaluates minimum LPIPS over ten rendered views rather than masked reconstruction error at the actual observation camera; CLIP image similarity is likewise too coarse to establish strict preservation. A camera-aligned visible-region evaluation is needed for this central claim.

An experimental inconsistency undermines the component attribution. Section 5.2 states that ExtremeOcc-3D uses RelaxFlow only in the geometry stage, while Section 4.3 introduces visibility masking in SLAT. Nevertheless, Figure 6a reports that removing this mask worsens ExtremeOcc-3D Point-FID from 81.1 to 92.3. The manuscript needs to clarify which stages and masks were actually used before this ablation can support the proposed mechanism.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete. The main ambiguity benchmark contains only 21 curated cases; its 100-case extension compares only against SAM3D and reports a small CLIP image gain, 0.839 to 0.845, without uncertainty. No seed variability or confidence intervals are given for the main results. The 32-person study omits sufficient details about presentation, randomization, voting, and aggregation to assess its large preference margin. Exact dataset selections, prior samples, baseline configurations, and sampling settings also need fuller specification. These weaknesses limit confidence in generalization and reproducibility despite the promising examples.

strengths: Significance: Text-controlled completion under fixed, ambiguous visual evidence is a useful problem. ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D explicitly distinguish category disambiguation from ordinary reconstruction and appearance editing.

Originality: Combining multiple visual proxies, relaxed prior attention, and visibility-aware velocity fusion is a plausible training-free adaptation of existing generators. Demonstrations on both SAM3D and TRELLIS support its practical applicability.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements over both backbones. With SAM3D, Point-FID improves from 100.38 to 81.11 and FID from 50.73 to 39.44. The additional baseline families in Appendix E and the 32-participant preference study provide useful complementary evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and qualitative comparisons are generally understandable. The manuscript supplies visibility-mask equations, default hyperparameters, runtime measurements, and explicit failures under conflicting conditions. The impact statement acknowledges misuse and bias; no material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—claimed equivalence is not established: The abstract and contributions claim a proof that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field. Appendix A.4 only assumes Lipschitz dependence on logits and bounds the magnitude of the resulting velocity perturbation. This neither establishes convolution of the velocity field nor proves attenuation of its high-frequency components. Smoothing flattened query/key indices also requires justification before identifying those frequencies with geometric structure versus instance detail.

Soundness—semantic error reduction is not proved: Proposition A.4 replaces the actual residual v_sem − Gσ*vθ with Gσ*(v_sem − vθ), dropping the signal-bias term v_sem − Gσ*v_sem. Gaussian smoothing does not exactly preserve nonconstant band-limited signals, and Assumptions A.2–A.3 do not quantify signal attenuation relative to noise reduction. Moreover, a reduction in the spatial L2 norm established through Parseval does not imply reduction along the particular trajectory used to define E_sem. These gaps invalidate the stated strict improvement guarantee.

Soundness—distributional claims exceed the stability argument: Lemma A.7 takes the time-varying α_t outside integrals over earlier times, although the implemented schedule changes and eventually becomes zero. Theorem A.8 also uses 1−α_max to weight observation error, which is not a valid general upper bound on its accumulated contribution. Even a repaired, smaller Wasserstein upper bound would not establish that the actual generated distribution is closer to ground truth, as claimed in Sections 3.2.2 and A.3.

Observation preservation is insufficiently supported: Keeping an observation-conditioned velocity unchanged does not impose a hard pixel reconstruction constraint, especially when it is evaluated at a shared state modified by prior guidance. Appendix D measures minimum LPIPS over ten rendered viewpoints rather than error restricted to observed pixels at the input camera. CLIP image similarity likewise measures semantic agreement rather than strict preservation. The central claim needs camera-aligned visible-region measurements and should be softened unless preservation is explicitly enforced.

Experimental consistency: Section 5.2 states that ExtremeOcc-3D uses RelaxFlow only in the geometry stage, whereas Section 4.3 introduces the visibility mask in SLAT. Nevertheless, Figure 6a reports a substantial ExtremeOcc-3D degradation when this mask is removed. The manuscript must reconcile which stages and masks were actually active. Figure 6b also reports default-N CLIP values that do not match Table 1, without explaining a different evaluation setting.

Evaluation and reproducibility: The original ambiguity benchmark contains only 21 manually curated cases; the 100-case extension compares only against SAM3D and reports a small CLIPimg gain of 0.006. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-seed results establish robustness to prior sampling. The selection of 264 ExtremeOcc cases from approximately 2,000 candidates is insufficiently specified, and the user study lacks presentation/randomization and aggregation details. Exact solver settings, attention-layer selection, token ordering and boundary handling, and benchmark identifiers/prompts are also needed for reliable reproduction.

Overall assessment: The practical combination and reported gains are worthwhile, but the theoretical understanding advertised as a central contribution remains unsupported, and the fidelity evaluation and ablation inconsistency prevent a technically solid acceptance recommendation.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements across both backbones. With SAM3D, Point-FID improves from 100.38 to 81.11 and CLIPtxt from 24.08 to 27.26. Qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful changes in unseen structure under different prompts.

Evaluation breadth: The paper includes component ablations, generated-versus-retrieved priors, additional baseline families, a 100-case ambiguity extension, and a 32-participant preference study. These provide encouraging evidence beyond selected visual examples.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is generally understandable, and the appendices provide useful metric definitions, visibility parameters, and runtime measurements. Appendix H candidly discusses incompatible observation/prior conditions; the impact statement acknowledges synthetic-content misuse and inherited biases.
weaknesses: Soundness—central equivalence is unsupported: The abstract and contributions claim a proof that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field. Appendix A.4 establishes only a Lipschitz bound on the change in velocity after modifying logits. This neither establishes convolution of the velocity field nor guarantees suppression of its high-frequency components. Smoothing token indices and smoothing over latent states are different operations, particularly through nonlinear softmax and subsequent network layers.

Soundness—the error-reduction proof has substantive gaps: Proposition A.4 replaces the actual error by Gaussian-smoothed error, omitting the signal-distortion term (I−Gσ)vsem. Band-limiting does not make a Gaussian preserve the signal exactly. Furthermore, reducing an unweighted spatial L2 norm via Parseval does not imply reducing the trajectory-restricted error defined in Eq. 3. The assumed separation between semantic signal and high-frequency error is also not empirically validated.

Soundness—the distributional guarantee is overstated: Lemma A.7 pulls the time-varying αt outside integrals over earlier times, which is invalid for the proposed cutoff schedule. Theorem A.8 also uses 1−αmax to weight observation error, although this is not an upper bound on its time-dependent weight. Independently, a smaller upper bound does not establish that the actual Wasserstein distance is smaller, as claimed in Section 3.2.2.

Observation preservation is neither enforced nor adequately measured: Keeping the observation branch unchanged does not impose a hard reconstruction constraint when its input state and generated geometry change. Appendix D uses minimum LPIPS over ten views rather than masked reconstruction at the observation camera, while CLIPimg measures semantic agreement with reference renders. These metrics cannot substantiate the repeated claim of strictly preserving visible pixels.

A key ablation conflicts with the stated implementation: Section 5.2 says ExtremeOcc-3D uses RelaxFlow only in the geometry stage, whereas Section 4.3 introduces the visibility mask in SLAT. Nevertheless, Figure 6 reports a substantial ExtremeOcc-3D degradation from removing that mask. The manuscript needs to reconcile which stages and masks actually produced these results.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete: No uncertainty estimates are reported for stochastic generation or prior selection. The user study lacks sufficient details on presentation randomization, voting protocol, and aggregation. Benchmark filtering from approximately 2,000 candidates to 264 cases is underspecified, as are solver settings, model checkpoints, and how the text-conditioned TRELLIS baseline is instantiated. Appendix D also does not clearly explain the reference set used for CLIPimg on AmbiSem-3D, which lacks unique target geometry.

Originality and overall assessment: The useful contribution is primarily the integration of visual proxy priors, attention smoothing, and scheduled spatial blending for amodal generation; related smoothing and guidance ideas are acknowledged. That integration could justify acceptance with reliable evidence, but the advertised theoretical contribution is not established and the central preservation claim is insufficiently tested. These are material weaknesses despite the promising empirical results.
